scenario.speaker: dana
scenario.briefing:
Neo Smart Living's RFP just landed — and before anyone in this agency scopes a method or prices a study, we define the problem. I had a discovery call with Neo's co-founder yesterday; my notes are in your inbox, close to verbatim.

Here's why I'm handing them to you raw: the most useful thing on that call was watching the client struggle. He told me what he *wants* — "reach." He could not tell me who his buyers are, and his own estimate of the answer moved twenty points inside one hour. That gap between what a client asks for and what a client actually needs diagnosed — that IS problem definition.

Three pages: classify what you heard, turn the client's wishes into research objectives, and pick the research questions that survive scrutiny. Do this well and the RFP response (your next round) practically writes itself.

inbox.subject: Discovery-call notes — read before you classify anything
inbox.body:
Notes attached, lightly cleaned. Two instructions:

1. Take the co-founder's words seriously but not literally. "We just need reach" is what he said; your job is to work out what has to be true before "reach" is even actionable.
2. Watch for the moment he declines to answer. Not every question a study COULD ask is a question research SHOULD answer — some decisions belong to the client, and a good analyst can tell the difference.

— Dana

attachments.title: Discovery call — Neo Smart Living co-founder (Dana's notes)
attachments.body:
**Growth to date.** Almost entirely referrals and word of mouth. No advertising at all until last month. Marketing hire is brand new; the first monthly ad budget is about to be allocated.

**On what Neo wants.** *"We just need reach — how do we get it in front of the right eyes?"* Asked what "the right eyes" means, he listed home office, guest room, premium storage, music/creative studio, multi-generational living — "all of them, really."

**On the segment breakdown.** Asked what share of sales comes from each use: *"We've never really dug into that internally."* First estimate: "over half is backyard." Later in the same call: "probably 70% backyard residential, 30% light-industrial." His own number moved twenty points in an hour.

**On competitors.** Believes there is no true direct competitor — "mostly importers reselling lookalikes."

**On promotion.** Asked which promotion method Neo would actually fund — sponsorships, digital, direct mail — he declined to commit: *"I'd need to talk to my partner before I answer that."*

**Also noted.** Referral sales are flattening while the new marketing budget sits unspent.

pages.title: Classify What You Heard
pages.intro: Five statements from the call. Tag each with what it is in the problem-definition cascade — symptom, underlying problem, decision alternative, or information need. The tags decide what happens next: symptoms get diagnosed, problems get researched, alternatives get evaluated, information needs get collected.

pages.title: From Wishes to Research Objectives
pages.intro: Three managerial objectives distilled from the call. For each, select the research objective a study can actually deliver — customer-answerable, specific, and free of crystal-ball forecasting.

pages.title: Pick the Research Questions
pages.intro: Seven candidate research questions are circulating. Three survive scrutiny; four fail it — one asks the future, one asks the client's own decision, one leads the witness, one belongs to internal records. Choose the three that survive.

guides.title: From Symptom to Research Question
guides.body:
**The cascade runs one direction.** Symptom → underlying problem → decision alternatives → information needs → research objectives → research questions. Clients arrive holding the top of the chain ("we need reach," "sales are flat"); research earns its fee by working downward before anyone acts.

- A **symptom** is a surface sign — observable, urgent-sounding, and not yet diagnosed. Treating a symptom directly ("buy ads!") is prescribing before diagnosing.
- The **underlying problem** is the unknown beneath the symptom. The reliable tell: the client cannot answer a basic question about their own market — and their estimate moves when asked twice.
- **Decision alternatives** are the actions on the table. Research does not choose among them; it supplies the facts that make the choice informed.
- **Information needs** are the specific facts required — each one traceable to an alternative it would inform.
- A **research objective** restates a managerial wish as something a study can deliver. The classic failure is the **crystal-ball question**: asking respondents to predict the future ("how much will sales increase?"). Customers can report what they do, use, feel, and expect — they cannot forecast outcomes for you.

**The difference habit.** At least one research question should compare groups ("do outdoor-active homeowners differ from others?") — difference questions are what turn a survey from a description into a targeting decision.

Round pointer: every statement on page 1 sits at exactly one level of this cascade, and the discovery notes contain one textbook example of each.

guides.title: The Customer-Answerable Test
guides.body:
Before a research question makes the questionnaire, it passes three filters:

1. **Could this respondent actually know it?** Customers know their own behavior, usage, preferences, expectations, and reactions. They do not know the future, other people's aggregate behavior, or anything inside the client's business. "How much will sales increase" and "what were Neo's segment revenues" both fail here — the first is a forecast, the second lives in Neo's own records (an internal secondary-data task, not a survey question).
2. **Is it research's question at all?** Some questions are decisions: "which promotion method should Neo fund" is answered in Neo's boardroom, informed by research but never delegated to it. When the client himself says "I'd need to talk to my partner," he is telling you which side of the line it sits on.
3. **Is it neutral?** A question that argues ("do you agree that next-day installation makes it the best value...") collects agreement, not information. If the wording contains the client's sales pitch, it fails.

Round pointer: of the seven candidates on page 3, exactly one fails each filter in a distinct, nameable way — and one more fails the neutrality filter. Name the failure before you deselect; that skill is the deliverable.
